\vspace{0.8em}

Recent papers report that a language model can take a wearable recording and
judge stress or mental effort. The recording is rarely shown on its own. It is
first turned into sentences: heart rate is high, the skin looks sweaty, the
pattern is the stress pattern. Those sentences already suggest the label. The
open question is whether the model is using the recording.

The project name refers to that possibility. A placebo resembles the treatment.
Here the prompt can resemble evidence.

The experiment uses public lab recordings in which the label is the assigned
task. Each recording is cut into minutes. Each minute is shown to a language
model with public weights, in three forms: the numbers, short sentences about
heart and skin, and a line plot. The recording is then replaced by noise, by
another person, or by nothing. A score that remains high does not depend on
that minute of physiology.

On the stress recordings, a simple logistic regression on ordinary heart and
skin features scores 0.92. The best language model, on the real minute, scores
0.60. A plot of the trace does no better than guessing, which is about 0.41
here, because always picking the common class is not a coin flip when the
classes are uneven. Noise does not always land on that line. On the averaged
heart trace, Qwen's noise score is 0.48. Qwen said ``stress'' on about a
third of those minutes, and chance for that answer rate on this score is
about 0.50. A flat line and a blank
prompt do sit on guessing, and so does another person who was doing something
else. A scrambled trace that keeps the spectrum still carries the answer for
the linear model, because several of the features are the level of the trace
and the size of its wiggles, which a phase scramble does not remove. A
recording from a different person who was under the same kind of stress carries
it too. When the model is reading sentences, it follows whatever class
information those sentences still contain. That sentence test has now been run.
On WESAD, Qwen loses little when the judgment words are removed, and loses a
great deal when those words are flipped. The numbers are in the sentence
section below.

A second experiment was requested at the last meeting: a comparison with a
recent paper on matched terms. Same public data, same kind of model, prompting
beside prompting, and fine-tuning beside fine-tuning. That paper uses daily
self-ratings of stress from 1 to 5, together with step counts and sleep. It
does not use these lab minutes. The comparison is reported separately, in
Section~\ref{sec:asked}, so the two scores are not placed in one table.

\section{Scoring}

Each minute is one question. The model does not write a paragraph. I look at
two letters and take the one it considers more likely. \texttt{A} is the
calmer class. \texttt{B} is the harder one. On WESAD that is calm versus the
speech. On MAUS it is the easy memory round versus the hard one. On CogWear it
is sitting quietly versus the color-word test.

The wording of the question was chosen on two people per dataset and then left
alone. Those two people are not in the scores. When a sentence says a value is
high or low, that word is set from everyone else, never from the person being
scored. The language models are not trained on these recordings. The only
trained model in the report is in the brown section, because that paper
trained one, and the request was to compare a fine-tune with a fine-tune.

The same procedure is applied to each dataset. A range in brackets is a 95\%
interval from redrawing the people one thousand times. The resampling unit is
the person, so one long recording does not dominate the interval.

\section{The score}

Every wearable score in the tables is macro-F1: the average of the two
per-class F1 scores, not the average of the two hit rates. The hit-rate
average is balanced accuracy, and it is exactly 0.5 for any answer that
ignores the label. Macro-F1 is not. On WESAD most minutes are calm, so always
saying ``calm'' scores about 0.41, and always saying ``stress'' scores about
0.23. A model that says each letter about half the time lands near 0.48. I
still call 0.41 guessing when I mean the common-class answer. It is not 0.50,
because the two classes are not the same size, and because this score moves
when the model changes how often it says the rare class.

The logistic regression is the one place a model is fit on these recordings.
It is trained on everyone except the person being scored, tested on that
person, and this is repeated until each person has been left out once. That is
the fair way to ask whether the features carry the class for a new person,
rather than for a person the model has already seen.

\section{The recordings, and why these ones}

I wanted a label I could point to in the lab protocol. Stress means the person
was doing the stressful task. It does not mean they wrote ``I feel stressed''
in a diary. If that sentence is already in the prompt, the heart trace is
optional, and the check is over before it starts.

The files also had to be public. Anyone should be able to download the same
recordings and rerun this. A private watch corpus cannot be checked, and I
cannot see whether a result used the pulse or some other field that was
already the answer.

Three tasks, not one. The claim in the papers is not ``this one dataset.'' It
is stress, and mental workload, and mental effort. If I only ran the dataset
where everything is easy, a success would be a success on that dataset. WESAD
is the one the field already uses for lab stress, and a simple model solves
it, so a language model near guessing there is failing a test that can be
passed. MAUS and CogWear are in the study so I cannot sell a WESAD result as a
general one. On those two the simple model is weak. That is useful. It means
there is less in the recording for anyone to read, and a language-model score
near guessing is not a surprise.

This is what one recording looks like. A person sits in a lab, wearing the
sensors, doing a timed task. I take 60 seconds. The next piece starts 30
seconds later, so neighboring minutes share half their samples. A piece never
crosses from the task into the rest period. The next section prints one of
those minutes the way the model actually receives it. A few seconds of the raw
heart trace show up again when I start swapping the recording out.

\textbf{WESAD} is fifteen people from the public stress dataset released by
the University of Siegen. They wear a chest belt and a wristband. The belt
records the electrical heart trace, skin conductance (how easily the skin
passes a tiny current, which rises with sweat), and breathing, 700 times a
second. The wristband records pulse with a light, 64 times a second, and skin
conductance more slowly. The hard class is a public speaking task, the Trier
Social Stress Test. The calm class is sitting quietly, plus watching a funny
clip. The files also contain a meditation block. I leave it out. It is not
the speech, and it is not the quiet sitting or the funny clip. Motion,
muscle activity, and temperature are in the files too. I do not use them. The
question is heart, sweat, and breath.

\textbf{MAUS} is twenty-two people doing a memory game, the n-back, with a
wrist pulse sensor. In the easy rounds (0-back) they respond to the item on
the screen now. In the hard rounds (2-back and 3-back) they have to remember
what came two or three items ago. The label is that difficulty, not a stress
rating. The files also contain a chest heart trace and a fingertip pulse. I
use the wrist pulse. That is the wearable in the claim, and it keeps this
dataset from becoming a second chest-ECG study. Resting recordings are in the
release and are not part of the task, so they are out.

\textbf{CogWear} is a wristband study from PhysioNet. The hard class is the
Stroop test: the word ``blue'' printed in red ink, and the person has to name
the ink. The other class is sitting quietly. I use the pilot group, ten people
with both pulse and skin conductance. An eleventh person is missing the
skin-conductance file in the public release, so that person is out. A second
cohort in the same archive played a different protocol, so I did not pool them
together. A headband EEG is in the files. I leave it out. A headset is a
different question from a watch.

I did not add daily self-ratings as a fourth wearable task. People scoring
their own day from 1 to 5 is the brown section, on a dataset called PMData,
because a published paper did that experiment and I was asked to meet it on
its own terms. Private industrial corpora, including the Fitbit data behind
SensorLM, are not here. There is nothing public to download.

\begin{center}
{\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}lccc@{}}
\toprule
\rowcolor{TableHead}
\textbf{Dataset} & \textbf{People included} & \textbf{Minutes} & \textbf{What the two classes are} \\
\midrule
WESAD & 15 of 15 & 1{,}042 & 731 calm / 311 stress \\
MAUS & 22 of 22 & 1{,}086 & 362 easy / 724 hard \\
CogWear & 10 of 11 & 114 & 39 rest / 75 Stroop \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
}
\end{center}

No minute was dropped for a missing sample. From each minute I compute the same
kind of summary a standard physiology toolbox would: heart rate, how much the time
between beats varies, skin conductance, and breathing where the belt recorded
it. The toolbox is NeuroKit2, version 0.2.13, and I have not edited it. The
logistic regression and the sentences are built from those same summaries.

\section{A simple model, before any language model}

I wanted a baseline that does not involve a language model at all. Before any
of those runs, I fit a logistic regression and a small decision tree on the
features. If a straight line through heart rate and skin conductance can
separate the classes, then the information is in the recording. A language
model that scores near guessing is leaving that information unused.

The shuffle ceiling is a check against luck. I shuffle the labels inside each
person, refit a thousand times, and take the score that 95\% of those
shuffles fall below. A real result has to clear that line.

\begin{center}
{\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}lccccc@{}}
\toprule
\rowcolor{TableHead}
\textbf{Dataset} & \textbf{Logistic regression} & \textbf{Small tree} & \textbf{Guessing} & \textbf{Shuffle ceiling} & \textbf{Useful?} \\
\midrule
WESAD (15 people) & 0.918 & 0.848 & 0.412 & 0.433 & Yes \\
MAUS (22 people) & 0.444 & 0.482 & 0.400 & 0.413 & Barely \\
CogWear (10 people) & 0.569 & 0.560 & 0.397 & 0.541 & Barely \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
}
\end{center}

WESAD is the dataset that can answer the question. The linear model is far
above guessing, so there is something for a language model to miss. MAUS and
CogWear are weak even for the linear model. On those two, a language-model
score near 0.4 does not mean much. When I later compress each result into one
ratio, those two will often be left blank, and I will show the raw gap instead.

\section{Language models on the real recording}

The text models are Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B. Both are open weights, which
means anyone can download them. The public plan originally named GPT-4.1. I
switched, because that account was capped at 50 requests a day. The plan has
a public note saying so.

``Every \(n\)th sample'' keeps one sample out of every few, so the minute
fits in a prompt. ``128 averages'' splits the minute into 128 bins and
averages inside each bin. ``Feature sentences'' are the lines from the
previous section. The two people set aside for wording are WESAD S2 and S8,
MAUS 015 and 023, and CogWear 4 and 8. Every minute in this table produced
a score.

The bold row is the best language-model result so far. Qwen, on WESAD, reading
the heart trace as 128 averages, with no examples in the prompt, scores 0.595.
The range sits above guessing. It does not come close to the logistic
regression at 0.918.

The feature sentences are close behind, at 0.584 [0.462, 0.699]. The range
starts above guessing and is wide. The sentence section scores this same
prompt again. That pass is 0.581 [0.460, 0.695] for Qwen and 0.278
[0.245, 0.316] for Llama, against 0.283 [0.247, 0.324] here. The two passes
agree in the second decimal.

Llama's two MAUS rows sit at 0.400 with a range that has no width. That is not
a crashed run. On every person in the table, Llama gave the same answer every
time. CogWear's ranges are wide because only 90 minutes are scored.

\section{Replacing the recording}

The prompts stay as they were. For each minute I swap the trace and score
again. Five swaps are there to remove the class. One is there for a different
reason.

\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Gaussian noise.} Random noise with the same average and spread
        as that sensor across the whole dataset. Stress and calm are not given
        their own noise.
  \item \textbf{Phase-randomized.} The sizes of the wiggles stay the same.
        That is the spectrum. Their timing is scrambled, so it no longer looks
        like that person's heartbeat.
  \item \textbf{Wrong person, wrong activity.} A minute from someone else, and
        I do not force it to be the same activity.
  \item \textbf{Flat line.} Every sample is replaced by the average of that sensor.
  \item \textbf{Nothing left.} The prompt says the signal was removed, and
        there are no digits left in it.
  \item \textbf{Same activity, other person.} Another person who was doing the
        same thing. This one is not trying to destroy the signal. It asks
        whether the model needs this recording, or whether stressed people
        simply look like each other.
\end{itemize}

\centering

    font=\footnotesize, inner sep=3pt, minimum height=0.78cm, text width=2.15cm
  },
  keep/.style={rung, fill=white, draw=Ask}
]

\node[rung, right=0.16cm of f] (d) {nothing\\left};

\end{tikzpicture}
\caption{Five ways of removing the class, and one swap that keeps it.
The lower box is not a destroyed signal. It is a different question.}
\end{figure}

\begin{figure}[!ht]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig_waveforms.pdf}
\caption{Eight seconds of chest ECG from one stress minute, WESAD person S10.
This is a different minute from the prompt example above, chosen so the four
traces can share a scale. Top is the recording. Below it: phase-randomized,
Gaussian noise, and a flat line at the same average. The person and the label
stay. Only the trace changes. On a shared scale the flat line is actually flat.}
\end{figure}

I scored every setup from the real-recording experiment on every replacement.
That is 120 runs, and none of them failed. The probability of each letter is
saved with every minute.

Before looking at the language models, I put the same features through the
same logistic regression. This says how much class information each
replacement still holds. I measure that. I do not assume a replacement is empty.

\begin{center}
{\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}lccc@{}}
\toprule
\rowcolor{TableHead}
\textbf{Replacement} & \textbf{WESAD} & \textbf{MAUS} & \textbf{CogWear} \\
\midrule
Gaussian noise & 0.412 & 0.400 & 0.486 \\
Phase-randomized & 0.880 & 0.405 & 0.458 \\
Wrong person, wrong activity & 0.411 & 0.405 & 0.380 \\
Flat line & 0.412 & --- & 0.397 \\
Signal deleted & --- & --- & --- \\
Same activity, other person & 0.954 & 0.494 & 0.773 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\end{center}

A dash means there was nothing to fit. A flat pulse on MAUS has no heartbeats,
so the features come out empty. Deleting the signal leaves no features on any
dataset.

The WESAD column is the one that says something. Noise, a flat line, and the
wrong person in the wrong activity all fall to 0.41, which is the common-class
score. A phase-randomized trace is still at 0.88. Another person doing the
same thing is at 0.95. That is not because the class lives in the spectrum.
Phase randomization keeps the value distribution of each minute, so the level
of skin conductance and the size of the wiggles stay put. Those are the
features the linear model is using. The correlation between a real WESAD
minute and its phase-randomized copy is 1.00 for the skin-conductance level
and 0.77 for mean heart rate. MAUS and CogWear never had a strong linear
score, and swapping the trace does not create one.

\begin{figure}[!ht]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig_ledger.pdf}
\caption{Logistic regression on each replacement. The missing orange bar, MAUS
with a flat line, is the empty-feature case in the table, not a score of zero.
The dashed line is guessing on WESAD.}
\end{figure}

The same replacements then went to the language models. The chart is Qwen on
WESAD, which is the only place a language model had clearly cleared the
common-class line on the real recording. I did run Llama on the replacements
as well. Its macro-F1 on the real WESAD sentences is 0.28, under the
common-class line, because it answers ``stress'' on almost every minute. The
ordering in its probabilities is not empty: the margin between the two letters
has an AUROC of 0.82 on those same minutes. Macro-F1 does not show that.

\begin{figure}[!ht]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig_surrogate_qwen.pdf}
\caption{Qwen3-8B on WESAD, people held out of the prompt wording. Left: the
heart trace as 128 averages (0.60 on the real recording). Right: the feature
sentences (0.58 on the real recording). Green is the real recording. Teal is a
replacement meant to remove the class. Brown keeps the activity and changes
the person. The legend is on the figure.}
\end{figure}

The right-hand panel is the sentence condition. On the real recording Qwen
scores 0.58. Sentences built from a phase-randomized trace score 0.70, above
the real recording. That rise is a shift in how often Qwen says ``stress'',
not a better reading of the minute. The ordering of the two letters is weaker
on the scrambled trace (AUROC 0.87) than on the real one (AUROC 0.94).
Sentences from another stressed person score 0.83, and the ordering stays high
(AUROC 0.92). Sentences built from noise fall to about 0.29, below the
common-class line, and the ordering goes to chance. A flat line and an empty
prompt sit on the common-class score. The left-hand chart, the raw trace, is
the one where noise does not: Qwen's noise score there is 0.48.

On the sentences, this agrees with the linear model in one respect. When the
sentences still contain the class, Qwen scores well even if the waveform is
no longer that person's. When the sentences are noise, or gone, Qwen falls to
the common-class line or below it. The raw trace is a smaller effect, and
noise there does not fall to 0.41.

\section{\texorpdfstring{\textcolor{Ask}{What you asked for}}{What you asked for}}
\label{sec:asked}

\AskedBox{%
\textbf{The answer, before the tables.}\\[0.35em]
The paper that matches the request is Health-LLM, from CHIL 2024.
Their task is a daily stress rating from 1 to 5. Lower error is better.\\[0.2em]
Prompting their model: they report 0.76. On the raw day-by-day list, this
rerun is 2.69, because the model says ``out of 5'' and the scoring rule writes
down 5. On their short prompt, the 14-day average, with the sampling decoder
their appendix calls the default, the error is 0.84, inside the band around
0.76.\\[0.2em]
Qwen, on their prompt, is at 0.80. Close to their prompting result, and worse
than always answering 3.\\[0.2em]
Fine-tuning every weight of their model on their data, with their 7B recipe,
brings the error to 0.44. Their paper says 0.38. An earlier run that trained
only a small add-on barely moved, and is kept as a record.\\[0.2em]
None of these numbers are wearable scores.%
}

At the last meeting you asked me to find recent papers, from a real venue, and
to compare like with like. If a paper only prompted the model, that result
sits next to prompting. If a paper fine-tuned, that result sits next to a
fine-tune of the same kind of model, on the same public data. A
classification score on WESAD does not belong next to an error on a 1-to-5
stress rating. This section is only the second kind of number.

SensorLM, from NeurIPS 2025, is about wearables and language models, but the
weights and the Fitbit recordings are not public, so it is not in the tables.
Other recent papers keep their labels private, or they are not language
models. I left those out for the same reason. Every paper in that reading,
and the earlier papers this study is written against, is named in
Appendix~\ref{app:papers}.

\subsection{\textcolor{Ask}{Their task}}

PMData is a public daily-life dataset. People wore a consumer tracker and,
each day, rated their stress from 1 to 5. The model sees two weeks of steps,
calories, resting heart rate, sleep, and that day's mood, and it has to give
that day's rating. The error is the average distance from the person's own
number. Always answering 3, on the 299 days I use as the test, is off by
0.401. That constant prediction is the reference for the errors below.

The model they released is MedAlpaca-7B. Their Table~3 is prompting, with no
examples in the prompt. Their Table~4 is the same model after it has been
fine-tuned on PMData. I kept those as two tables.

\subsection{\textcolor{Ask}{Prompting only}}

I used their prompt, and a test set of 299 days that was fixed before the run.
The scoring rule was fixed too: read the first number in the answer. I did not
change the rule when the number looked wrong.

A lot of MedAlpaca's answers say ``out of 5'' or ``out of 10.'' The rule
records 5 or 10. A stress rating only goes to 5, so those answers are far
from a typical day. That is why this rerun sits at 2.69 while the paper says
0.76. I left the rule as it was.

Their own paper also writes the two weeks as one average per sensor, not as
the raw list, and the appendix sets sampling as the default decoder. I ran
that prompt, temperature 0.4, three seeds, same first-number rule, same 299
days. The errors are 0.823, 0.853, and 0.846. The mean is 0.841, and the
spread is 0.016. Their published band is \(0.76 \pm 0.1\), so 0.841 is inside
it. It is not the same point as 0.76. The model says 2 or 3, not ``out of 5.''

Qwen, given the raw list, answers ``Answer: 3.'' Its error is 0.795, near
the paper's prompting result, and still worse than the constant answer of 3.

Llama, given the same words, does not answer with a stress rating. It writes
a short Python program, and the rule reads a step count out of that program.
The error is about 2,650. The scoring rule was not changed.

\begin{center}
{\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}llcc@{}}
\toprule
\rowcolor{Ask!15}
\textbf{Row} & \textbf{Model} & \textbf{What was done} & \textbf{Average error} \\
\midrule
Their Table 3 & MedAlpaca-7B & no examples & $0.76 \pm 0.1$ \\
This rerun, raw list & MedAlpaca-7B & day-by-day list, greedy & $2.689 \pm 0.038$ \\
This rerun, their average & MedAlpaca-7B & 14-day average, sampling & $0.841 \pm 0.016$ \\
Our model, their prompt & Qwen3-8B & no examples, same rule & $0.795 \pm 0.020$ \\
Our model, their prompt & Llama-3.1-8B & no examples, same rule & $2654 \pm 43$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\end{center}

\noindent Lower is better. This table is prompting. It is not a WESAD score,
and it is not the fine-tuning table below.

\FloatBarrier
\subsection{\textcolor{Ask}{Fine-tuning only}}

Their Table~4 says that fine-tuning MedAlpaca on PMData brings the error down
to 0.38.

I fine-tuned the same model on the training examples they released. One
training example also appeared in the locked test set, so I dropped it. The
training file has 653 examples. I did not oversample, because they never
published the rule for it. I also skipped their 100-step warmup. With only
653 examples at batches of 128 there are 18 update steps, and a warmup that
long would never reach the learning rate.

Their 0.38 uses their own test split. My number uses the 299 days I had
already locked. Same model, same task, same error. I am not claiming the two
test lists are the same list.

The first attempt trained only a small adapter, an add-on of a few million
weights, at their learning rate of \(2\times 10^{-5}\). It barely moved. The
adapter starts at zero, and after 18 small steps its largest weight was about
0.0002. Scored on the raw question it said ``out of 5'' and landed at 2.697,
the same as the model before training. That number stays as a record of a
run that did not train.

Their appendix says the parameters themselves are updated. So the second run
trains every weight: 3 epochs, batches of 128, learning rate
\(2\times 10^{-5}\), cosine schedule. It is scored on the template it was
trained on, which ends at ``Response.'' The paper used four large GPUs. This
machine has one 48~GB card, so the weights are stored in a 16-bit format and
the optimizer keeps its running averages in 8 bits. The training loss fell
from 1.84 to 1.04 over the 18 steps.

After that run, every answer reads ``The predicted stress level is N.'' With
the sampling decoder from their appendix, three seeds, the error is 0.448,
0.435, and 0.442. The mean is 0.442, and the spread is 0.007. Their paper says
0.38. Greedy decoding says 3 on all 299 days, which is exactly the constant
answer, at 0.401.

\begin{center}
{\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}llcc@{}}
\toprule
\rowcolor{Ask!15}
\textbf{Row} & \textbf{Model} & \textbf{What was done} & \textbf{Average error} \\
\midrule
Their Table 4 & MedAlpaca-7B & fine-tuned on PMData & 0.38 \\
This rerun & MedAlpaca-7B & every weight trained, sampling & $0.442 \pm 0.007$ \\
This rerun & MedAlpaca-7B & every weight trained, greedy & 0.401 \\
First attempt & MedAlpaca-7B & small adapter, did not train & 2.697 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\end{center}

\noindent Lower is better. This table is fine-tuning. It does not get compared
with the prompting table, and it does not get compared with WESAD.

\begin{figure}[!ht]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig_asked.pdf}
\caption{The two tables, drawn. Left is prompting. Right is fine-tuning.
Lower is better. The dashed line is the error from always answering 3.
On the left, the raw list is 2.69 and the 14-day average with sampling is 0.84.
On the right, training every weight brings the error to 0.44 with sampling.
Llama is not on the chart. Its error is about 2{,}650, because it wrote a
program and the scoring rule read a step count. It is in the prompting table.}
\end{figure}

\AskedBox{%
\textbf{What I take from this.}
On the raw list, with their model and a scoring rule fixed in advance, I do not
get 0.76. The model says ``out of 5.'' On the 14-day average, with sampling,
the error is 0.84, inside their published band and not equal to 0.76.
Training every weight on their data brings the error to 0.44, near their 0.38.
Almost every answer after training is 3, and always answering 3 scores 0.401.
Qwen, which was not trained on their data, lands near their published prompting
error and still loses to always answering 3.
Llama does not answer the question that was asked.
This says something about running their experiment. It does not say whether a
language model can read a WESAD minute.%
}

\section{The sentence test}

The prompts stay the ones frozen in September. Only the sentences change.
The original wording here is a second scoring of the feature-sentence row
above, not a different prompt.
Three wordings of the same numbers: as written, with the judgment words
removed, and with those words flipped. Removing them leaves the number and
its percentile among the other people. Flipping them swaps ``elevated'' with
``reduced,'' and ``stress-typical'' with ``calmer-typical,'' and leaves the
number alone. Both models, all three datasets, every minute scored. No
failures.

The plan filed before these runs made two predictions. Removing the judgment
words should cost more than half of whatever advantage the original wording
had over the shuffle floor. Flipping the words should change the predicted
letter on more than 40\% of minutes. If the original wording was not
convincingly above that floor, the first prediction is left unscored.

Read the figure left to right. Dark is the original wording. Teal is the
same numbers with the judgment words removed. Brown is those words flipped.
The whiskers are the interval from redrawing people. The dashed line is
guessing.

\begin{center}
{\footnotesize
\begin{tabular}{@{}llccc@{}}
\toprule
\rowcolor{TableHead}
\textbf{Model} & \textbf{Dataset} & \textbf{As written} & \textbf{Words removed} & \textbf{Words flipped} \\
\midrule
Qwen & WESAD & 0.581 [0.460, 0.695] & 0.554 [0.441, 0.662] & 0.313 [0.224, 0.403] \\
Qwen & MAUS & 0.485 [0.438, 0.529] & 0.399 [0.345, 0.448] & 0.507 [0.466, 0.546] \\
Qwen & CogWear & 0.475 [0.393, 0.504] & 0.542 [0.426, 0.612] & 0.597 [0.513, 0.658] \\
Llama & WESAD & 0.278 [0.245, 0.316] & 0.230 [0.227, 0.233] & 0.230 [0.227, 0.233] \\
Llama & MAUS & 0.400 [0.400, 0.400] & 0.400 [0.400, 0.400] & 0.503 [0.450, 0.553] \\
Llama & CogWear & 0.479 [0.375, 0.640] & 0.404 [0.392, 0.417] & 0.404 [0.392, 0.417] \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
}
\end{center}

\begin{figure}[!ht]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig_sentence_test.pdf}
\caption{The three wordings. Left is Qwen. Right is Llama. Dark bars are the
sentences as written. Teal bars have the judgment words removed. Brown bars
have those words flipped. The dashed line is guessing.}
\end{figure}

The last column is the one to use when the question is whether flipping the
words changed the letter.

\begin{center}
{\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}lccc@{}}
\toprule
\rowcolor{TableHead}
\textbf{Share of minutes that change} & \textbf{WESAD} & \textbf{MAUS} & \textbf{CogWear} \\
\midrule
Qwen & 63\% [52, 74] & 71\% [65, 77] & 72\% [51, 91] \\
Llama & 3\% [1, 6] & 27\% [15, 40] & 8\% [0, 18] \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
}
\end{center}

Qwen on WESAD loses about 17\% of its margin when the words are removed. The
plan said more than half, so that prediction does not hold there. On MAUS the
whole margin goes against the filed chance floor, so the filed prediction
holds. A chance floor matched to how often Qwen says the hard class on MAUS is
0.499, and the original wording scores 0.485, under that floor. The MAUS
result holds only under the filed floor. CogWear's original wording was not
clearly above the floor, so that prediction is not scored. Flipping the words
changes more than 40\% of Qwen's minutes on all three datasets. It does not do
that for Llama. Counting the judgment words, with no language model, already
scores 0.74 on WESAD, above Qwen's 0.58, and Qwen's margin tracks that count
(Spearman 0.84). SensorLM's statistical sentences were not part of this run.

\section{One ratio per setup}

The replacement charts already show what happens when the recording is
swapped. The sentence test above is the second of the three filed
predictions. The third, flipped words changing more than 40\% of minutes,
is now scored as well.

The ratio is now computed, outside this PDF, in
\texttt{results/sds\_card/}. In words, it is how much of the gap between the
real recording and the locked chance floor disappears when the recording is
replaced:
\[
\frac{\text{real} - \text{replacement}}{\text{real} - \text{chance}}.
\]
If the real recording was never convincingly above that floor, the ratio is
left blank. Seventy-five of the one hundred null cells are blank for that
reason. Where a ratio is printed, it is the filed one, including values above
1 and below 0. Those happen when the replacement scores on the wrong side of
the chance floor, which this score does easily when the model changes how
often it says the rare class.

The raw-number and plot rows have been scored again, with the probability of
each letter saved. The new scores sit within 0.009 of the September ones.
The largest move is Qwen on CogWear, every nth sample, 0.576 to 0.585. The
sentence rows were already saved. None of the twenty real setups moved enough
to treat the September number as a different run.

The one cell that clears chance on the raw trace is Qwen on WESAD, reading
the heart trace as 128 averages. The ratio there is not below 0.3.

\begin{center}
{\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}lcc@{}}
\toprule
\rowcolor{TableHead}
\textbf{Replacement} & \textbf{Ratio} & \textbf{Real minus replacement} \\
\midrule
Gaussian noise & 0.644 & 0.116 [0.048, 0.180] \\
Phase-randomized & 0.344 & 0.064 [0.010, 0.121] \\
Wrong person, wrong activity & 0.450 & 0.082 [0.026, 0.145] \\
Flat line & 1.041 & 0.186 [0.141, 0.239] \\
Nothing left & 1.041 & 0.186 [0.141, 0.239] \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
}
\end{center}

A ratio above 1 means the replacement scored below the chance floor. The
bracket is the paired interval from redrawing people.

undefined: the real recording never cleared the chance floor, so no ratio
is printed.}
\end{figure}

\begin{figure}[!ht]
\centering

\caption{The ordering of the two letters, against macro-F1, on the real
recording. A point high and to the left is a model that ranks the minutes
well and still picks the common letter too often.}
\end{figure}

through October 2026. A paper enters the brown tables only when the dataset,
the task, the kind of model, and the score can sit next to Health-LLM. The
second list is older. Those papers are why the wearable study exists. They
are not PMData numbers, and they are not in those tables.
